description.en:
As early as age 14, Rizal valued education for enabling the youth to contribute to society. He would later express this sentiment at 18, during his second year at the Universidad de Santo Tomas (UST), through his winning piece, “A La Juventud Filipina.”

The sonnet implores the Filipino youth to “display in splendor your magnificent talents… and break the heavy chains that hold down your artistic genius” for “the Spaniard offering a splendid crown.” The “heavy chains” mentioned do not refer to the Spanish repression of the Filipino genius, as “the Spaniard” is described as “loving” and “wise.”

But as Paul Arvisu Dumol, PhD and Clement C. Camposano, PhD wrote in The Nation as Project: A New Reading of Jose Rizal’s Life and Works, the “heavy chains” refer instead to the Filipinos’ timidity, as seen in the poem’s first line, “Grow, oh timid flower,” which is sometimes translated as “Raise your smooth brow.”

Further, in Rizal’s novel El Filibusterismo, timidity is identified as a detrimental trait among Filipinos.

## References

Dumol, Paul Arvisu and Camposano, Clement C. The Nation as Project: A New Reading of Jose Rizal’s Life and Works. 2018.
description.fil:
Sa murang edad na 14, pinahalagahan na ni Rizal ang edukasyon dahil binibigyang-daan nito ang kabataang makapag-ambag sa lipunan. Ihahayag niya ang damdaming ito nang maglaon sa edad 18, sa kanyang ikalawang taon sa Universidad de Santo Tomas (UST), sa pamamagitan ng kanyang nagwaging akdang “A La Juventud Filipina.”

Hinihiling ng soneto sa kabataang Pilipino na “ipamalas sa karingalan ang inyong mga dakilang talino… at lagutin ang mabibigat na tanikalang pumipigil sa inyong talinong masining” para sa “Espanyol na nag-aalay ng maringal na korona.” Ang binanggit na “mabibigat na tanikala” ay hindi tumutukoy sa panunupil ng Espanya sa talinong Pilipino, yamang inilarawan ang “Espanyol” bilang “mapagmahal” at “matalino.”

Ngunit gaya ng isinulat ni Paul Arvisu Dumol, PhD at Clement C. Camposano, PhD sa The Nation as Project: A New Reading of Jose Rizal’s Life and Works, tumutukoy ang “mabibigat na tanikala” sa pagkamahihiyain ng mga Pilipino, gaya ng makikita sa unang linya ng tula, “Lumago, o mahihiyaing bulaklak,” na isinasalin din kung minsan bilang “Itaas ang makinis mong noo.”

Dagdag pa, sa nobela ni Rizal na El Filibusterismo, tinutukoy ang pagkamahihiyain bilang mapaminsalang katangian sa mga Pilipino.

## Mga Sanggunian

Dumol, Paul Arvisu and Camposano, Clement C. The Nation as Project: A New Reading of Jose Rizal’s Life and Works. 2018.
description.de:
Schon mit 14 Jahren schätzte Rizal die Bildung, weil sie der Jugend ermögliche, zur Gesellschaft beizutragen. Mit 18, im zweiten Jahr an der Universidad de Santo Tomas (UST), gab er dieser Haltung in seinem preisgekrönten Gedicht „A La Juventud Filipina“ Ausdruck.

Das Sonett ruft die philippinische Jugend auf, „in vollem Glanz deine herrlichen Gaben zu zeigen… und die schweren Ketten zu brechen, die dein künstlerisches Genie niederhalten“ – für „den Spanier, der eine prächtige Krone bietet“. Die erwähnten „schweren Ketten“ meinen nicht die spanische Unterdrückung des philippinischen Geistes, denn „der Spanier“ wird als „liebevoll“ und „weise“ beschrieben.

Doch wie Paul Arvisu Dumol, PhD, und Clement C. Camposano, PhD, in The Nation as Project: A New Reading of Jose Rizal’s Life and Works schrieben, verweisen die „schweren Ketten“ vielmehr auf die Zaghaftigkeit der Filipinos, wie die erste Zeile des Gedichts zeigt: „Wachse, o zage Blüte“, manchmal auch übersetzt als „Erhebe deine glatte Stirn“.

Im Übrigen wird die Zaghaftigkeit in Rizals Roman El Filibusterismo als schädlicher Wesenszug unter den Filipinos benannt.

## Literatur

Dumol, Paul Arvisu and Camposano, Clement C. The Nation as Project: A New Reading of Jose Rizal’s Life and Works. 2018.
